access-platform.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings); ISO 14122-2
access-platform.drawn: Plan view: a rectangle (often partly hatched to show grating) with the leg positions marked at the corners and the ladder or stair access drawn at one edge, labelled with its top-of-grating elevation (TOG EL +…).
access-platform.notes: On P&IDs an access platform is sometimes noted beside a valve as "accessible from platform", not drawn. A larger outline with grid lines is a deck-module.

jacket.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (structural elevation); ISO 19902 / API RP 2A
jacket.drawn: Elevation: a tapering (battered) frame from the seabed up to the deck with horizontal levels and X or K bracing, the sea level drawn as a wave line and the mudline at the bottom; in plan, circles at the leg positions.
jacket.notes: Not on P&IDs. Risers and conductors are drawn along the jacket face; the deck above is deck-module.

datasheet.form: Jacket structural drawing / design basis (ISO 19902, API RP 2A-WSD)

bridge.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (structural elevation)
bridge.drawn: Elevation: two horizontal chords joined by a zig-zag Warren truss, with a pinned support (triangle) at one end and a sliding support (roller circle) at the other; in plan, two parallel lines between the platform outlines labelled with the bridge name.
bridge.notes: On P&IDs a bridge appears only as off-page arrows "via bridge to RP" on lines that cross it. The sliding end is what lets the platforms move relative to each other.

helideck.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings); CAP 437 markings
helideck.drawn: Plan view: an octagon (or circle) with the touchdown / positioning circle and the letter H at the centre, the D-value and maximum mass written on it, plus the obstacle-free sector chevron.
helideck.notes: The H in a circle on an octagon is unambiguous. The helicopter refuelling package and the windsock are separate items around it.

steel-column.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (structural plan / section)
steel-column.drawn: Plan view at a grid intersection: the column section (an H or I shape, a square for SHS, a circle for CHS) on a square base plate with anchor bolt circles, tagged with its section size.
steel-column.notes: Not on P&IDs. On framing plans columns sit on the dash-dot grid; a beam is drawn as a single line between them with its section written along it.

steel-beam.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (structural elevation / framing plan)
steel-beam.drawn: Elevation: two parallel flange lines with end plates (or fin plates) at each end; on framing plans a single thick line between columns with the section (e.g. IPE 300, TOS EL +28.000) written along it.
steel-beam.notes: Not on P&IDs. A beam drawn thicker on a plan is usually a primary girder.

grating-panel.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (floor plan hatch)
grating-panel.drawn: Plan view: an area filled with close parallel lines (the bearing bar direction), sometimes a cross-hatch, with the panel outline; solid plate is drawn plain or with a checker-plate hatch.
grating-panel.notes: Only on structural and layout drawings. The hatch direction shows the span direction of the bearing bars.

handrail.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (elevation); ISO 14122-3
handrail.drawn: Elevation: top rail and knee rail on posts with a toe plate at the bottom; on plans a line just inside the deck or platform edge with small post marks (or crosses), and a gate drawn as a short swing arc.
handrail.notes: On plans it looks like a wall line; the post marks and the location at the edge identify it. Not on P&IDs.

cable-tray.drawn: Cross-section: stacked open trays (U-channels) on cantilever arms from a post; on cable routing plans two parallel lines with the tray width and level (e.g. 600 W, TOT EL +3.2) and short diagonals or rung marks.
cable-tray.notes: Only on electrical and instrument layouts. Two parallel lines with rungs in plan can be confused with a ladder; trays run along routes and carry width notes.

caisson.standard: ISO 10628-2 / P&ID convention for deck-hung caissons
caisson.drawn: A long vertical pipe or open-bottom vessel hanging from the deck through the sea-level line, with the inlet or pump column entering at the top; labelled as seawater lift, firewater, disposal or sump caisson.
caisson.notes: Pumps drawn inside it are vertical-turbine-pump or diesel-firewater-pump. A riser is a pipe line (with ESDV) that continues to a subsea pipeline, not an open-ended caisson.

datasheet.form: Caisson datasheet / structural drawing (NORSOK P-001, ISO 19902)

module-frame.standard: Layout plan convention (structural / plot plan drawings) (structural elevation); ISO 19901-6 lifting
module-frame.drawn: Elevation: a rectangular frame with intermediate floor and X-bracing on the faces, padeyes at the top corners; on plot plans a module boundary rectangle with its tag and weight.
module-frame.notes: On P&IDs a module or package boundary is a dash-dot rectangle around the equipment it carries.

datasheet.form: Module structural drawing / weight report (ISO 19901-6, DNV-ST-N001)

shell-and-tube-exchanger.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001; TEMA type designation
shell-and-tube-exchanger.drawn: Horizontal shell (long rectangle or capsule) with the channel head at one end and the tube bundle drawn as a line or U inside; tube-side nozzles on the channel, shell-side nozzles on the shell. Many legends draw a circle with a zig-zag through it, or two interlocking circles, for any exchanger, with the TEMA type (AES, AEU, BEM, AKT) written beside it.
shell-and-tube-exchanger.notes: The tag letter E and the TEMA type confirm it. A shell with an enlarged dome and a weir is a kettle (AKT). A box with a fan is an air cooler; a frame with many plates is a plate exchanger; two pipes with a return bend is a hairpin.

datasheet.form: TEMA shell-and-tube heat exchanger specification sheet (API 660)

air-cooled-exchanger.drawn: Rectangle (the finned-tube bundle, often with a zig-zag tube line inside) with a fan below it (forced draft) or above it (induced draft), drawn as a propeller or bow-tie on a shaft to a motor (circle with M); louvres as a row of slanted lines over the bundle.
air-cooled-exchanger.notes: The fan with its motor tells it from a shell-and-tube exchanger. The number of bays and fans is written beside it (e.g. 2 bays × 2 fans).

datasheet.form: API 661 / ISO 13706 air-cooled heat exchanger datasheet

plate-heat-exchanger.drawn: Rectangle (the plate pack) crossed by several parallel lines (the plates), between a fixed frame plate and a pressure plate, with all four connections on the fixed frame end; some legends draw a box with a diagonal zig-zag.
plate-heat-exchanger.notes: Many parallel lines inside a compact box = plate exchanger. A solid block with channels is a PCHE.

flare-boom.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 (flare tip) / layout convention for the boom
flare-boom.drawn: On the flare P&ID: the flare header ending at a flare tip symbol (a short stack with a flame outline on top), with pilot gas and ignition lines; on layouts an inclined boom outline from the platform edge to the tip.
flare-boom.notes: Inclined boom = offshore flare boom; a vertical stack from grade is a flare-stack. A stack with no flame symbol is a cold vent.

flare-stack.drawn: A tall vertical stack with a flame outline at the tip and the flare header entering at the base, often with the molecular or velocity seal drawn as a bulge below the tip and pilot lines alongside.
flare-stack.notes: With a flame at the top it is a flare; without one it is a cold vent stack. A ground flare is a box or fence enclosure with burners.

fired-heater.drawn: A box (radiant section) with a zig-zag process coil inside, burners drawn as small flames or triangles at the floor, a tapering convection section and a stack on top; the fuel gas line goes to the burners.
fired-heater.notes: Zig-zag coil inside a firebox with burners = fired heater. An electric heater has a resistance element and a terminal box; a TEG reboiler is a horizontal capsule with a fire tube.

vent-stack.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 (vent to atmosphere, flame arrester)
vent-stack.drawn: A line turning up into an open-ended stack with an arrow or "to atmosphere" at the top, often with a flame arrester (box with parallel lines) at or near the tip; labelled VENT or VS-.
vent-stack.notes: No flame symbol: a cold vent. An open-ended small-bore line ending in a goose-neck or "TO ATM" is just a vent connection, not a stack.

datasheet.form: Vent stack datasheet (API 521 dispersion, ISO 16852 flame arrester)

electric-heater.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 / IEC 60617 heating element
electric-heater.drawn: A horizontal shell with a resistance element (zig-zag) drawn inside it and a terminal box on the flange end; the power supply comes from a thyristor controller and the process inlet and outlet are on the shell.
electric-heater.notes: The zig-zag element plus a terminal box tells it from a shell-and-tube exchanger. On P&IDs a TIC with a TY / thyristor box and a high-temperature trip (TSHH on the element) usually accompanies it.

datasheet.form: Electric process heater datasheet (IEC 60079-7 / ASME VIII-1)

hairpin-exchanger.drawn: Two parallel horizontal pipes (the legs) joined by a return bend at one end, an inner pipe shown running through both, tube-side connections at the open ends and shell-side nozzles on each leg.
hairpin-exchanger.notes: The U-shaped double-pipe outline tells it from a shell-and-tube (single shell with a channel). Stacked hairpins in series are drawn as several hairpins joined by short lines.

printed-circuit-heat-exchanger.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 (generic exchanger box); no specific PCHE symbol
printed-circuit-heat-exchanger.drawn: Usually a generic heat-exchanger box or rectangle with crossing flow lines and four nozzles (hot side on the ends, cold side on the faces), tagged E- and noted "PCHE" or "compact / diffusion-bonded".
printed-circuit-heat-exchanger.notes: There is no standard PCHE symbol: rely on the note or the datasheet. Common in gas dehydration, compression aftercooling and dew-point control where space is tight.

cooling-tower.drawn: A box (or tapering hyperbolic outline for natural draft) with a fan stack on top (propeller in a short cylinder), the hot-water distribution near the top, crossed lines for the fill, air inlets low on the sides and the cold-water basin at the bottom.
cooling-tower.notes: The fan on top plus fill and basin tell it from an air-cooled exchanger (tube bundle, no water basin). Onshore only.

gate-valve.drawn: Two triangles meeting at their points (bow-tie) across the line, unfilled. A short stem with a T on top marks the handwheel; a gear operator is sometimes drawn as a small box on the stem.
gate-valve.notes: A filled dot at the centre means globe; a circle means ball; a bar through the centre means butterfly. A fully black bow-tie is the same valve normally closed (NC). LO / CSO / LC / CSC written beside it are locked or car-sealed positions, not a different valve.

ball-valve.drawn: Bow-tie across the line with an open circle at the centre where the triangle points meet. Manual valves may show a stem with a T or a lever.
ball-valve.notes: Open circle = ball; filled dot = globe; plain bow-tie = gate. The same body under a square actuator with an S or a fail-close note is an ESDV / SDV / XV (esd-valve). Some legends write FB / RB beside it for full or reduced bore.

esd-valve.standard: ISA 5.1 (actuator) on an ISO 10628-2 ball valve body; IEC 61511 SIS final element
esd-valve.drawn: Ball-valve bow-tie (circle at the centre) under a rectangular spring-return piston actuator, usually with a small box marked S (solenoid) on the actuator and "FC" beside the body. The tag bubble reads ESDV, SDV or XV.
esd-valve.notes: Same symbol with FO and tag BDV is a blowdown valve. A dome actuator means a control valve; a circle with M means an MOV. Limit switches (ZSO / ZSC) and the SOV are accessories of this valve, not separate items. Some legends draw a gate body instead of a ball; the ESDV tag decides.

datasheet.form: Actuated on/off valve datasheet (API 6D / ISO 14313 + actuator sheet, IEC 61508 SIL data)

blowdown-valve.standard: ISA 5.1 (actuator) on an ISO 10628-2 ball valve body; API 521 depressuring
blowdown-valve.drawn: Actuated ball valve like an ESDV (rectangular spring-return actuator, solenoid box) but marked FO, usually drawn black-filled or marked NC because it is normally closed. It sits on a line from the vessel or compressor to the flare header, often followed by a restriction orifice (RO).
blowdown-valve.notes: Tell it from an ESDV by the FO mark, the flare (FL / BD) line it sits on and the BDV tag. The restriction orifice downstream is drawn as a pair of short bars across the line (like an orifice plate) tagged RO.

datasheet.form: Blowdown valve datasheet (API 6D + actuator sheet, API 521 depressuring case)

control-valve.standard: ISA 5.1 / ISO 10628-2 (control valve with diaphragm actuator)
control-valve.drawn: Bow-tie body with a stem up to a dome (half circle on a flat base): the spring-diaphragm actuator. A tag bubble such as LV, PV, FV, TV, PCV, LCV, FCV, TCV sits next to it, often with FC / FO / FL and a bypass globe valve drawn around it.
control-valve.notes: Dome = diaphragm actuator (control valve). A rectangle = piston actuator (usually on/off: ESDV / SDV / XV / BDV). A circle with M = MOV. A self-acting regulator (PCV with no signal line, impulse line to the pipe) uses the same body with a sensing line instead of a positioner signal.

datasheet.form: Control valve specification sheet (IEC 60534-7 / ISA-75.25 / ISA-TR20.00.01)

pressure-safety-valve.drawn: Angle body: one triangle pointing up from the inlet below and one pointing in from the outlet on the side, meeting at a right angle, with a zig-zag spring rising from the meeting point to a short cap line. The set pressure and orifice letter (e.g. 3K4, set 42 barg) are written beside it.
pressure-safety-valve.notes: The spring zig-zag tells it from a check valve or a plain angle valve. A rupture disc (PSE) is drawn as a curved disc between flanges with no spring. Size code like 3K4 means 3" inlet, K orifice, 4" outlet. The outlet line goes to the flare header (FL / RV) or to atmosphere; on a pilot-operated PSV a small pilot box is drawn beside the spring. ISA codes here: PSE = rupture disc.

datasheet.form: Pressure relief valve datasheet (API 526 / API 520, ISA-TR20.00.01 form)

globe-valve.drawn: Bow-tie across the line with a solid black dot at the centre where the triangles meet, and a handwheel stem with a T. Often found as the bypass around a control valve or as a throttling valve.
globe-valve.notes: Solid dot = globe; open circle = ball; plain bow-tie = gate. A bow-tie with a dome actuator is a control valve, which is a globe body too: the actuator decides.

datasheet.form: Globe valve datasheet (API 623 / BS 1873 / ASME B16.34)

swing-check-valve.drawn: Bow-tie with one triangle filled black (the downstream half) and often a small arrow showing the free-flow direction. Some legends draw a single triangle pointing at a bar instead.
swing-check-valve.notes: P&IDs rarely distinguish swing, dual-plate and piston checks: read the valve code in the line class or the valve datasheet. Flow is allowed in the direction the arrow (or the open triangle) points.

datasheet.form: Check valve datasheet (API 6D / BS 1868 / ASME B16.34)

dual-plate-check-valve.drawn: Non-return symbol (a triangle pointing at a bar across the line) squeezed between two flange marks, because the wafer body sits between the pipe flanges. Many legends just use the general check-valve bow-tie with one half filled.
dual-plate-check-valve.notes: Wafer-type (API 594) is usually only visible from the valve code or a "W" / "DP" note. Treat any check-valve symbol on a line ≥ NPS 3 in water or gas service with a wafer valve code as this component; otherwise use swing-check-valve.

datasheet.form: Wafer check valve datasheet (API 594 Type A)

butterfly-valve.drawn: Bow-tie with a straight bar through the centre at right angles to the line (the disc), often with a dot at its middle. Older legends draw two vertical lines with a diagonal between them.
butterfly-valve.notes: Bar through the centre = butterfly; circle = ball; filled dot = globe; two close parallel bars = knife gate. Common in seawater, cooling and firewater lines.

plug-valve.drawn: Bow-tie with a small rectangle (the plug) at the centre where the triangles meet; manual plug valves show a wrench or T on the stem.
plug-valve.notes: Legends vary: some draw a plug valve as a bow-tie with a filled triangle-in-circle, others as a ball valve with "P" or "PLUG". Check the legend; the valve code in the line class confirms it.

motor-operated-valve.standard: ISA 5.1 (electric motor actuator) on an ISO 10628-2 gate body
motor-operated-valve.drawn: Valve bow-tie with a stem to a circle containing M: the electric motor actuator. The tag bubble is usually MOV, XV or HV, and the valve fails in place (FL / FAI).
motor-operated-valve.notes: Circle with M = motor actuator; dome = diaphragm (control valve); rectangle = piston or spring-return (ESDV / BDV). A square with "M" is used by some legends for the same thing.

datasheet.form: Valve datasheet (API 600) + electric actuator datasheet (ISO 5210 / IEC 60034)

needle-valve.drawn: Small bow-tie on an instrument, sample, vent or drain line (NPS 1 and below) with a stem ending in a pointed needle at the seat; often unlabelled, next to a gauge or transmitter.
needle-valve.notes: Usually drawn smaller than line valves and attached to instrument tubing. Many P&IDs show instrument root and manifold valves only as a generic small gate symbol, or not at all; treat them as detail unless asked.

datasheet.form: Instrument valve datasheet (MSS SP-99 / ASME B16.34)

check-valve-piston.drawn: Check-valve bow-tie (downstream half filled, flow arrow) with the globe-pattern dot at the centre on some legends; on most P&IDs it is drawn exactly like any check valve.
check-valve-piston.notes: Identify it from the valve code (lift / piston check, usually small-bore or high-pressure, NPS 2 and below) rather than the symbol. Swing and dual-plate checks use the same base symbol.

datasheet.form: Check valve datasheet (BS 1868 / API 602 / ASME B16.34)

knife-gate-valve.drawn: Gate-valve bow-tie with a thin slab (two close parallel bars) drawn through the centre, standing proud of the body, and a handwheel stem.
knife-gate-valve.notes: Legends vary: some show a knife gate as a plain gate bow-tie with "KG" written beside it. A single bar through the centre is a butterfly. Typical in slurry, sand, drain and low-pressure water service.

horizontal-separator.drawn: Horizontal capsule (rectangle with semi-elliptical ends). A 3-phase separator shows a weir plate inside and a water boot below; a 2-phase separator a mesh pad at the gas outlet; a KO drum is plain.
horizontal-separator.notes: Vertical capsule = vertical-separator. Long capsule with closure door at one end = pig-launcher. A horizontal capsule with filter elements and a lower sump barrel = filter-separator.

vertical-separator.drawn: Vertical capsule (tall rectangle with elliptical heads) with a mesh pad or vane pack drawn as a hatched band near the top, gas outlet at the top, inlet on the side and liquid outlet at the bottom; scrubbers are tall and slim.
vertical-separator.notes: A taller capsule with trays or packing is a column; one with cartridges and a tube sheet is a cartridge filter. Scrubbers, KO drums and inlet separators all use this symbol: the internals and service decide.

column.drawn: Tall vertical capsule with trays drawn as short horizontal lines alternating from the left and right walls (segmental trays), or a section with crossed diagonals for packing; overhead at the top, bottoms at the bottom, feed and reflux on the side.
column.notes: Alternating tray lines or an X-crossed packed bed = column (TEG contactor, absorber, stabiliser). A shorter vessel with only a mesh pad is a vertical-separator.

datasheet.form: Column / tower datasheet (ASME VIII-1; tray or packing sheet)

filter-separator.drawn: Horizontal vessel with filter elements (dashed vertical lines) in the first section, a vane or mesh pack in the second, a smaller liquid sump barrel below joined by downcomers, and a quick-opening closure (thick bar) at the filter end.
filter-separator.notes: The second barrel underneath and the filter elements tell it from a horizontal separator. A vertical housing with cartridges is a cartridge-filter.

cartridge-filter.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 (filter: vessel with a dashed filter medium line)
cartridge-filter.drawn: Vertical housing on legs with a tube sheet line and the cartridges as dashed lines (or a single dashed line across for the filter medium), a quick-opening or bolted closure at the top, and a PDI / PDT across inlet and outlet.
cartridge-filter.notes: ISO and PIP draw any filter as a vessel crossed by a dashed line; coalescers add "COALESCER". A horizontal vessel with a sump barrel is a filter-separator; a Y in the line is a y-strainer.

storage-tank.drawn: Flat-bottomed vertical rectangle on grade with a shallow cone (triangle) or dome roof, inlet near the top, outlet near the bottom; floating-roof tanks show the roof as a line inside the shell. Breather / PVRV and emergency vents sit on the roof.
storage-tank.notes: Flat bottom on grade = atmospheric tank (API 650); a capsule with elliptical heads = pressure vessel. A circle on legs is a sphere.

spherical-tank.drawn: A circle standing on legs that touch it at the equator, with top and bottom nozzles; often with a water-spray (deluge) ring drawn around it.
spherical-tank.notes: Circle on legs = sphere. A circle on its own in a line could be a pump or an instrument bubble: check for legs and size.

air-receiver.drawn: Plain vertical capsule on legs with no internals, inlet low on one side, outlet high on the other, a PSV on top and an auto-drain at the bottom, on the instrument-air or nitrogen system.
air-receiver.notes: An empty vertical vessel on an IA / UA / N2 line is a receiver; with a mesh pad and liquid outlet it is a vertical-separator.

desander.drawn: A cyclone (short cylinder over an inverted cone) with a tangential inlet on the side and the overflow out of the top, the underflow dropping through two isolation valves into a sand accumulator vessel below that is dumped periodically.
desander.notes: A cone over an accumulator on a well stream = desander. Produced-water hydrocyclones are horizontal multi-liner vessels without the accumulator. ISA codes here: LT = sand; XV = dump.

datasheet.form: Desander datasheet (ASME VIII-1; API 6A-class end connections)

bullet-tank.drawn: Horizontal capsule with hemispherical or 2:1 heads standing on two saddles, liquid inlet and vapour balance on top and liquid outlet at the bottom; a deluge ring or water-spray line is often drawn around it.
bullet-tank.notes: A horizontal capsule with no internals or boot in LPG / NGL storage service is a bullet; separators show a weir, boot or mesh pad. Spheres are circles on legs.

datasheet.form: Pressure storage datasheet (ASME VIII-1 / API 2510 / NFPA 58)

slug-catcher.drawn: An inlet header splitting into several parallel, slightly sloped long pipes (fingers), with gas risers from the top of the fingers to a gas header and the liquid draining to a liquid header at the low end.
slug-catcher.notes: Parallel sloped fingers between headers identify a finger slug catcher; a vessel-type slug catcher is drawn as a large horizontal separator.

christmas-tree.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 valves; API 6A / API RP 14C wellhead conventions
christmas-tree.drawn: A vertical run of valves above the wellhead: lower master (manual), upper master (SSV, with an actuator box), a cross with the production wing valve (often actuated) and the choke (bow-tie with a diagonal arrow) on the side, and the swab valve and tree cap on top. The SCSSV is shown below the wellhead as a valve with a control-line note.
christmas-tree.notes: A single vertical valve stack with a side wing and choke is a tree; a stack of boxes with rams is a BOP; a stack of spools with only annulus outlets is the wellhead housing. Injector trees have the wing on the injection line with the flow arrow into the well. ISA codes here: XV = wing.

datasheet.form: Wellhead and christmas tree datasheet (API 6A: PSL, PR, temperature and material class)

choke-valve.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 valves; API 6A / API RP 14C wellhead conventions (adjustable choke: valve body with a diagonal arrow)
choke-valve.drawn: An angle-body valve (side inlet, bottom outlet) or an in-line bow-tie with a diagonal arrow through it meaning adjustable restriction; a fixed (positive) choke has no arrow and a bean size note. Tagged HCV, PCV, FCV or CK.
choke-valve.notes: The diagonal arrow = variable choke. An angle body with a spring is a PSV, not a choke. A globe control valve with a dome actuator can also do choking duty; then it is control-valve.

production-manifold.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 valves; API 6A / API RP 14C wellhead conventions
production-manifold.drawn: Two (or three) parallel headers, production and test, with each well flowline arriving through a check valve and branching to every header through its own valve, so one well can be routed to test while the rest go to production.
production-manifold.notes: The repeating slot pattern (one inlet, one valve per header) is the signature. A single header with branches is just a header pipe. Test header size is usually smaller; HP / LP headers may both be present.

pig-launcher.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 / API 6D pig trap convention
pig-launcher.drawn: An oversized barrel with a quick-opening closure (thick bar) at one end, a reducer to the pipeline size, the trap (isolation) valve on the pipeline, and a kicker (or bypass) line from the barrel round the trap valve; a pig signaller (XI / ZS) on the line. Receivers are drawn the same way, mirrored.
pig-launcher.notes: The closure plus reducer plus kicker line is unmistakable. A plain horizontal capsule is a vessel. Launcher or receiver is decided by flow direction.

datasheet.form: Pig trap datasheet (ASME VIII-1 / ASME B31.4 / B31.8)

bop-stack.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 valves; API 6A / API RP 14C wellhead conventions; API 16A / API 53 BOP schematic
bop-stack.drawn: A vertical stack of boxes: the annular preventer on top (tapered or rounded), ram preventers (rectangles with rams drawn from both sides, labelled pipe / blind / shear), and a drilling spool with the choke and kill lines and their valves leaving each side.
bop-stack.notes: Rams drawn as boxes with side rams distinguish a BOP from a christmas tree (bow-tie valves). Only on drilling or well-control schematics, not process P&IDs.

riser.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 / pipeline P&ID convention
riser.drawn: The topsides line turning down through the deck to sea level and below, with the riser ESDV (actuated valve with an S box) above the deck, an insulating joint (two close bars with a gap) and an off-page note "to / from subsea pipeline"; the sea level is often drawn as a wave line.
riser.notes: An open-ended pipe hanging into the sea (pump or sump) is a caisson. Pipeline pig traps sit just upstream on the topsides.

datasheet.form: Riser design basis / line list (API RP 2RD, ISO 13623)

wellhead-control-panel.standard: ISA 5.1 (panel; hydraulic signal lines marked L) / API RP 14C
wellhead-control-panel.drawn: A rectangle (local panel) labelled WHCP with hydraulic signal lines (marked with L) running to each well's SCSSV, SSV and wing valve actuators, and an ESD / fusible-loop input.
wellhead-control-panel.notes: One hydraulic line per actuator per well. A box with only one hydraulic supply line is an HPU (hydraulic power unit), not the WHCP.

datasheet.form: Wellhead control panel datasheet (API RP 14C / ISO 10418)

drilling-derrick.drawn: Elevation: a tall tapering lattice tower on a box substructure with the drill floor line between them and the crown block on top; in plan, the rig footprint rectangle with the well centre(s) marked as circles and slot numbers.
drilling-derrick.notes: Never on process P&IDs except as a tie-in box (mud, cement, utilities). The BOP and wellhead below the floor are separate items.

wellhead-housing.standard: ISO 10628-2 / PIP PIC001 valves; API 6A / API RP 14C wellhead conventions
wellhead-housing.drawn: A stack of rectangles (casing head at the bottom, casing and tubing head spools above) on the conductor, each with side annulus outlets carrying gate valves and gauges; a blind flange or tree adapter on top.
wellhead-housing.notes: Only annulus side outlets and no wing / choke means a wellhead without a tree (suspended well, or below a BOP). With a valve stack and choke on top it is a christmas-tree. ISA codes here: PI = annulus; PT = annulus.
